issues.legal_issue: A compromise adjusting a claim in a suit or appeal must be in writing and signed by the parties, even when the settlement is reached during a court hearing and recorded in the proceedings.
material_facts: During the hearing of an appeal, one side offered to pay a sum on a future date in full and final settlement, and the other side accepted the offer in a statement before the court.
The statements formed part of the court proceedings, but the compromise terms were not reduced to writing and signed by the parties.
Before the payment date, the accepting party resiled from the proposed compromise.
The court had to decide whether the appeal could be disposed of on the basis of that compromise.
issues.conclusion: The compromise could not be given effect to as an adjustment under Order XXIII Rule 3 because it was not in writing and signed by the parties. The appeal had to be heard and decided on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXIII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as amended, an adjustment by lawful agreement or compromise requires a completed agreement in writing and signed by the parties, including when the compromise is made during a suit or appeal hearing. The amendment was intended to prevent false or frivolous pleas of oral compromise that could delay proceedings. The agreement must be capable of being embodied in a decree. The contrary view in Manohar Lal v. Surjan Singh was overruled. The rule’s Explanation excludes agreements that are void or voidable under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, from being lawful compromises.

predicates.suit_or_appeal_adjustment_proceeding: The court is deciding whether a claim in a suit or appeal has been adjusted.
predicates.claimed_agreement_adjustment: A party relies on an agreement or compromise as having adjusted the claim.
predicates.written_signed_terms: The terms of the agreement or compromise were reduced to writing and signed by the parties.
predicates.claimed_agreement_adjustment_cannot_be_r: The court cannot record the claimed agreement as an adjustment and must decide the proceeding on its merits.

issues.definition: When a party claims that an agreement adjusted a claim in a suit or appeal, the court cannot record that adjustment and must decide the proceeding on its merits if the terms were not written and signed.

issues.legal_issue: A promise of future payment that is repudiated before payment is not satisfaction of the plaintiff’s claim under the satisfaction limb of Order XXIII Rule 3.
material_facts: The proposed compromise required payment on a future date by bank draft.
Before that date, the party entitled to receive payment resiled from the proposed compromise.
The promised payment had not been made, so the case concerned a proposed agreement rather than completed satisfaction of the claim.
issues.conclusion: The proposed compromise did not fall within the satisfaction limb of Order XXIII Rule 3; the party relying on it could only rely on the agreement limb, which required written and signed terms.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXIII Rule 3 distinguishes an adjustment by agreement or compromise from satisfaction of the plaintiff’s claim by the defendant. Satisfaction need not be proved by a written agreement signed by the parties; it may be established by a receipt, bank payment, or other evidence. The court decides whether satisfaction occurred on the evidence. A promise of future payment that is repudiated before payment does not establish such satisfaction.

predicates.suit_or_appeal_adjustment_proceeding: The court is deciding whether a claim in a suit or appeal has been adjusted or satisfied.
predicates.future_payment_promised: A party promised to pay or perform the claim at a future time.
predicates.promise_resiled_from_before_payment: The promise was repudiated before the promised payment or performance occurred.
predicates.proposed_future_payment_is_not_actual_cl: A promise of future payment that is repudiated before performance is not satisfaction of the claim.

issues.definition: A promised future payment that is repudiated before performance does not count as satisfaction of the claim in a suit or appeal.
